lessons.title: Why people are the #1 way in
lessons.body:
Most breaches don't start with a clever exploit - they start with a person
clicking something. Phishing (a fake email), smishing (text), vishing (phone),
and pretexting (a believable story) all target the human, not the machine. You
can't patch a person, so the defense is recognition + process. That's this layer:
learn the tells, and the alarm goes off in your head before you click.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a phishing email - read the RAW headers
lessons.body:
The pretty email hides the truth; the raw headers tell it. Always read the source.
  Inspect it on either OS:
    Linux/macOS/WSL:  cat suspicious.eml        grep -i 'from\|spf' suspicious.eml
    PowerShell:       Get-Content suspicious.eml  (or:  type suspicious.eml)
                      Select-String -Path suspicious.eml -Pattern 'From|spf'
  What to check, in order:
    From: vs Return-Path/Reply-To  -> do they match? A mismatch is a red flag.
    The link's REAL href vs its display text -> hover/read source, never trust text.
    The sending domain -> is it the real one, or a lookalike? (next lesson)

lessons.title: SPF, DKIM, DMARC - did the mail prove who it is?
lessons.body:
Three checks that say whether a 'From' is forged. They show up in the
Authentication-Results header:
  SPF   - was the sending server ALLOWED to send for that domain?  (pass/fail)
  DKIM  - is there a valid cryptographic signature from the domain?  (pass/none)
  DMARC - given SPF+DKIM, does the domain's policy say to trust it?  (pass/fail)
A real message from a well-run domain passes all three. 'spf=fail ... dkim=none
... dmarc=fail' on a From you trust means the sender is almost certainly spoofed.
This is the single fastest tell in email triage.

lessons.title: Lookalike domains and homoglyphs
lessons.body:
Attackers register domains that LOOK like yours so a glance trusts them:
  - a letter swapped for a twin:  lakefront  ->  1akefront  (one for L),
    rn for m, 0 for o, vv for w.  These are 'homoglyphs'.
  - an extra word:   lakefront-paper-support.com   (real domain never had it)
  - a different TLD:  lakefront-paper.co  instead of .com
Defense: read the domain character by character, right-to-left from the TLD.
The real registered domain is the last two labels before the TLD - judge THAT,
not the subdomain the attacker put your real name in (portal.lakefront.evil.com).

lessons.title: Mail flow and MX records (how the letter arrives)
lessons.body:
When mail is sent to you@lakefront-paper.com, the sender looks up the domain's
MX record (a DNS entry naming the mail servers) and delivers there. You can see
a domain's MX with:  nslookup -type=mx lakefront-paper.com  (works on both OSes;
Linux/WSL also has  dig mx lakefront-paper.com). Why it matters: the 'Received:'
chain in the headers should end at YOUR real MX hosts. A message that entered
through servers that aren't your MX, claiming to be internal, is suspect.

lessons.title: Recon: what attackers learn before they knock
lessons.body:
Before any email or scan, attackers gather. Defenders check the same sources to
see what they're exposing:
  - PUBLIC CODE (GitHub): a repo pushed with a hardcoded password, API key, or
    internal hostname is a gift. Real breaches start here constantly. Defense:
    scan your own repos for secrets, rotate anything that ever leaked, keep
    secrets in env/secret-stores, never in the code or git history.
  - SHODAN (shodan.io): a search engine that scans the whole internet and indexes
    what every exposed device/service answers - open ports, banners, product and
    version. Attackers search it for 'this product, this version, exposed'.
    Defense: search Shodan for YOUR own IPs/org and close what shouldn't be public.
  The lesson: your attack surface includes everything you've published - code,
  DNS, and anything plugged into the internet - not just the app you meant to ship.

quiz.q: Fastest signal that a 'From' address is forged?
quiz.why: SPF/DKIM/DMARC failures mean the sender couldn't prove it owns the domain.

quiz.q: '1akefront-paper.com' (digit one, not L) is an example of...
quiz.why: A character swapped for a look-alike twin to pass a quick glance.

quiz.q: Where should you judge whether a domain is really yours?
options: the last two labels before the TLD
quiz.why: portal.lakefront.evil.com is really evil.com; judge the registered domain.

quiz.q: A hardcoded password pushed to a public GitHub repo is...
options: fine if the repo is small
a common real-world breach entry point
quiz.why: Attackers scan public code for secrets; rotate anything that ever leaked.

quiz.q: What does Shodan let someone do?
options: search the internet for exposed devices/services and versions
quiz.why: It indexes what internet-connected services expose - check your own exposure.
